title: Basic Sandwich

jokes.text: He apparently used nothing but gold to assemble his circuitry, believing it to be a better conductor of human emotion. It was a weird time. The Bionic Woman won an Emmy.
jokes.setup: Earnest exposition about Borchert's eccentric belief that gold conducts human emotion — played completely straight.
jokes.punchline: 'It was a weird time. The Bionic Woman won an Emmy.' — the deadpan non-sequitur contextualizes absurdist history with a ridiculous pop-culture credential.
jokes.explanation: Classic Community cold-open narration humor: a straight-faced documentary aside that uses a specific, verifiable absurdity (The Bionic Woman Emmy) as cultural shorthand for 'this era had no standards.' The economy is superb — one sentence does all the work. Not quite a 9 because the character integration is weak (any narrator could say it), but it's a genuinely well-crafted comedic aside.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Russell Borchert, an eccentric inventor who believed that gold conducts emotions better than any other metal, spent his life savings on a suit made entirely of gold leaf.

jokes.text: Some people said he hid his money using a portal to another dimension. Those people were on LSD.
jokes.setup: Narrator lists increasingly wild theories about where Borchert hid his money, treating each one with equal documentary gravitas.
jokes.punchline: 'Those people were on LSD.' — the blunt, clinical dismissal breaks the documentary register perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Structurally very clean: the setup carefully escalates to the absurd claim, and the punchline is a single-sentence anchor back to reality. The deadpan delivery of 'Those people were on LSD' as a neutral factual statement rather than a joke is exactly the right register. High economy score — four words do maximum work.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: The Bionic Woman won an Emmy. That's how weird the '70s were.

jokes.text: This adventure I usually have to force upon us. It is falling into our laps. We're like the Goonies.
jokes.setup: The group has just found evidence of a secret hidden area of Greendale with possible treasure. Everyone is excited.
jokes.punchline: Abed frames their adventure in pure narrative/movie terms — 'I usually have to force upon us' acknowledges his own role as the group's adventure-instigator, and 'We're like the Goonies' is his highest compliment.
jokes.explanation: Deep character integration — Abed openly acknowledging his meta-role within the show as the person who engineers the group's adventures is a layered joke that only Abed can deliver. It works on two levels: as a Goonies reference and as genuine self-awareness. The rewatch bonus is real because viewers who've seen the whole series appreciate how accurately self-critical this is.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Some people said he hid money using a portal to another dimension.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Those people were idiots.

jokes.text: - Except our story tracks logically. - And we're not talking over each other. - Everyone talks at the same time. Sorry. - Can you stop?
jokes.setup: Abed says they're like the Goonies. Someone adds 'except our story tracks logically.'
jokes.punchline: The group immediately begins talking over each other — directly contradicting the claim — and then can't stop doing so even while acknowledging it.
jokes.explanation: A self-eating joke with perfect structural irony: the claim 'we're not talking over each other' immediately causes everyone to talk over each other. The escalation of meta-awareness ('Can you stop?') while they're still doing it makes it pay off twice. Well-constructed and efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: The Goonies? Please. That movie is objectively inferior to our adventure.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: Jeff, you can't just say that. The Goonies is a classic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Our production design was 40% more authentic. Our child actors showed 60% more range. And our soundtrack was performed by an actual orchestra, not just the theme from Cops.

dialogue.speaker: Troy Barnes
dialogue.line: We don't have a theme song.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Exactly. We're that good.

jokes.text: The entire school is shaped like a penis.
jokes.setup: The group lays out blueprints of the school looking for a hidden stairwell. The blueprints reveal the layout.
jokes.punchline: One character announces the school is shaped like a penis when everyone else is focused on the stairwell clue.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the audience expects a plot revelation, gets a phallic joke instead. Functional and gets a laugh, but it's a fairly cheap visual gag. The setup is good (everyone leaning over blueprints), the execution is a bit lazy. Exists primarily to set up the stronger follow-up joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We don't talk over each—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know, we're actually really good at—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: —other anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: —listening to each other.

jokes.text: What the hell does your penis look like?
jokes.setup: Someone says the school is shaped like a penis. Jeff redirects attention to the actual clue on the blueprints — a cluster of buildings.
jokes.punchline: 'What the hell does your penis look like?' — Jeff's withering dismissal of the penis comment doubles as an inadvertent anatomical question.
jokes.explanation: This is a premium comeback: Jeff uses a rhetorical put-down that simultaneously dismisses the previous joke AND makes a funnier one. It's very Jeff — condescending, quick, and unexpectedly crude from someone who presents as suave. High quotability because it works completely out of context. The structure is excellent: setup (penis comment), redirect (Jeff points to the stairwell), then the punchline recontextualizes both. Earns its near-8 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, is anyone else seeing what I'm seeing in these blueprints?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? It's just the campus layout.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly. The campus layout. Look at it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's a penis.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? No it's not!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've seen enough to know where this is going.

jokes.text: Obviously a cluster of buildings. Let's have a laugh at the freak.
jokes.setup: Jeff deflects the phallic comment by pointing out it's just a cluster of buildings on the blueprint.
jokes.punchline: Jeff sarcastically invites everyone to mock the person who saw a penis — 'Let's have a laugh at the freak' — which also implies everyone secretly agrees but won't say so.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's sardonic persona is well-deployed here — his invitation to 'laugh at the freak' is simultaneously mean and self-aware. It extends the previous two-joke run effectively. Character-consistent and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey, my penis doesn't look like a strip mall.

jokes.text: Serial killers and people that hide treasure leave weird little clues.
jokes.setup: The group searches for the missing stairwell and Abed offers narrative context for why they might find clues.
jokes.punchline: The casual equivalence of 'serial killers and people that hide treasure' as a unified category is the joke — delivered with complete Abed sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Abed: he draws on genre knowledge (crime thrillers, adventure stories) and conflates two genres without irony. The character integration is high because this observation could only come from someone who processes reality through narrative categories. Clean economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, I think we should all just accept that some buildings are going to be shaped like penises.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Or we could just make fun of you for saying that.

jokes.text: Check it out. Look at the bottle held by the school's first and least acceptable mascot, Big Chief Drunky.
jokes.setup: The group searches for clues about the hidden stairwell. Someone spots a painting of the school's original mascot.
jokes.punchline: 'Big Chief Drunky' — the casual revelation that Greendale's first mascot was an offensively named Native American caricature, presented with zero ceremony.
jokes.explanation: Community has always been willing to name institutional racism directly and play it for uncomfortable laughs. 'Big Chief Drunky' is a great gag name — specific, appalling, and plausible for a 1970s community college. The 'least acceptable' qualifier shows the writers are self-aware. Solid dark-subversive humor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, what's the name of the school mascot again?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The Greendale Human Beings.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my god.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... that's actually terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I never thought about it like that.

jokes.text: Is Duncan okay? He'll live, but his food's gonna taste like burnt aluminium for a while.
jokes.setup: Professor Duncan has just been electrocuted by wires in the wall. Someone asks if he's okay.
jokes.punchline: The casualness of 'he'll live' followed by the hyper-specific, oddly clinical detail about food tasting like burnt aluminium — a funny, specific side effect delivered as if it's a known medical fact.
jokes.explanation: The specific sensory detail ('burnt aluminium') elevates this above a generic 'he'll be fine' joke. It's funny because it's simultaneously too specific and too casual — the speaker clearly has personal experience with electrocution. Good dark-subversive energy.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Desperate attempt to find meaning in random electrical sparks

jokes.text: It's pronounced 'aluminium.' See, he's fine.
jokes.setup: Duncan has just been electrocuted. Someone notes his food will taste like 'burnt aluminum.'
jokes.punchline: Duncan, supposedly incapacitated, immediately corrects the American pronunciation of 'aluminium' — the pedantic correction IS the proof of life.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: the previous line sets up Duncan's incapacitation AND inadvertently creates a linguistic setup. Duncan's first post-electrocution words being a British spelling/pronunciation correction is deeply character-specific — he's British, he's academic, and he's petty enough to correct people while semiconscious. The follow-up 'See, he's fine' is the ideal button. Economy is near-perfect: three words, two jokes (he's alive; he's characteristically pedantic). Would score 9+ if Duncan were more of a lead character — the callback is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: It's pronounced 'uh-LOO-mi-num'.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: See? I'm fine.

jokes.text: Oh, look, it's Jeff Winger, fun police — here to pull over our smiles — because our mouths have tinted windows.
jokes.setup: Jeff tells the group to stop and admit the treasure hunt is over.
jokes.punchline: Britta constructs an extended metaphor — 'fun police pulling over smiles with tinted windows' — which is simultaneously clever and try-hard, which is perfectly Britta.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on a character level more than a pure comedy level: Britta is trying too hard with the extended metaphor, which IS her character. 'Fun police' alone is good; pushing it to 'tinted windows' is Britta overreaching. The fact that she overreaches is the actual joke. High character integration because a confident wit would stop at 'fun police.' This is Britta going too far and not knowing it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, look. A treasure hunt is just an elaborate way to waste time. We could be doing something productive.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, smiles are like cars with tinted windows.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You can't see what's going on inside, but you know something is.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Exactly. And that's why we smile.

jokes.text: Britta and I are getting married. / Married? Well, you're gonna need way more doves than this.
jokes.setup: Jeff announces out of nowhere that he and Britta are getting married — a complete shock to the group.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's immediate response isn't emotional or logical — it's a practical wedding-planning observation about dove quantities, delivered as if this is the salient issue.
jokes.explanation: Shirley's response is perfectly in character — she's the religious Southern woman who immediately goes to wedding logistics, and the specificity of 'doves' (not flowers, not a dress) is a great choice. The structure also works because it treats a dramatic revelation as mundane, which deflates the moment in a satisfying way.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We're getting married!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, have you thought about the doves?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What doves?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: For the wedding. You need doves. Lots of them.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've been calling around. Nobody has enough doves. Nobody. We might have to cancel.

jokes.text: What does this look like, an hour-long episode of The Office?
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta announce they're getting married. The group reacts with chaos — pickaxing, electric zapping, an absurd scene.
jokes.punchline: Abed dismisses the melodrama by comparing their current situation to an hour-long episode of The Office — a competing workplace mockumentary — implying their show has LOWER stakes and doesn't deserve that runtime.
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp meta joke: Abed name-drops a competitor/peer show as a negative comparison, implying Community is scrappier/weirder/less prestige than The Office's big dramatic moments. The 'hour-long episode' specification is key — it's the distinction between normal TV drama and special-event drama. Only Abed, who literally processes life through television, can make this joke. It lands as self-deprecating but also defensive — they're different, not lesser. Near-excellent joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We should probably acknowledge the marriage announcement.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, but have you seen The Office's wedding episodes? They're like two hours long.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So I'm not sitting through that.

jokes.text: There's pick-axing and electric zapping. Don't even acknowledge it. We are not acknowledging this.
jokes.setup: The group is reacting to the Jeff-Britta engagement announcement
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Britta immediately go into denial mode, explicitly refusing to process their own announcement — the meta-joke being that the show itself is refusing to commit to this plot development
jokes.explanation: The self-aware refusal to process the plot beat is very Community. It's both character comedy (Jeff's emotional avoidance) and meta-commentary (the show knowing this is a dramatic escalation it doesn't want to commit to).

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Does anyone have rope?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Excuse me? What is that supposed to mean?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? I just need rope.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: You think I don't have rope? I always have rope!

jokes.text: Who's got rope? / I'm offended by that question.
jokes.setup: The group discovers a trapdoor and needs to descend into it. Someone asks who has rope.
jokes.punchline: Hickey — the gruff, seen-it-all shop teacher/enforcer — is offended by the QUESTION, implying he obviously has rope and finds it insulting to be asked to confirm it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy: Hickey is a man who always has rope and considers the question an insult to his competence and preparedness. The joke is entirely in the gap between the question and the response — no elaboration needed. Five words do complete character work. High economy and character integration scores are justified.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, we need to figure out which key opens this door.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Have you tried them in order?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: In order? What order? Which one is first?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The first key you try.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But how do I know which one I'm going to try first until I try it?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: He's got a point.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly. So the first key is whichever key I try first, which means there is no first key until I've already tried a key, at which point it becomes the first key retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or you could just try them.

jokes.text: Richie and Carl from the school board. That's right. We got names.
jokes.setup: The school board antagonists arrive at the door to stop the group.
jokes.punchline: One of them announces their names and immediately notes 'we got names' — acknowledging that as recurring minor antagonists they've been nameless this long, and treating having names as an achievement.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever meta joke that rewards long-time viewers: these two characters have appeared multiple times as unnamed obstacles. The self-awareness that 'getting names' is a milestone for a TV character — and the pride with which it's delivered — is a sharp piece of meta comedy. Only works fully in context of the whole series but gets a chuckle even cold. The 'that's right' as a moment of minor triumphalism is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Be careful with the door, Richie.

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I got this.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Here, have a drink.

jokes.text: Well, it's never the first one, so we can cancel this one out. / I guess now this is the first one, so it should be the next one.
jokes.setup: Richie and Carl are trying to find the right key to open the door. They're trying to apply logic to key selection.
jokes.punchline: Their reasoning is a perfect loop of self-defeating logic — eliminating the first key because 'it's never the first one' and then calling the next key 'the first one' by the same logic, so it must also be eliminated.
jokes.explanation: Classic bureaucratic-idiot logic — the circular reasoning is well-constructed and plays on the universal frustration of key selection. It characterizes Richie and Carl as people who apply false systems to simple problems. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Oh, hello there! Lovely day, isn't it?

jokes.text: Get out of the way. / Richie, be careful. / Don't worry. I've been drinking.
jokes.setup: Carl and Richie can't get the key to work. Carl takes charge to try himself.
jokes.punchline: Richie's warning to 'be careful' is dismissed by Carl with 'Don't worry, I've been drinking' — presented as a reassurance, not a concern.
jokes.explanation: The inversion is excellent: drinking is offered as a QUALIFICATION rather than a hazard. The economy is superb — four words as punchline. Very quotable because it works in many contexts. These two minor characters are doing strong comedic work in this sequence.

jokes.text: Oh, hello. Would you like some tea? / The tea is swell.
jokes.setup: The school board men finally break into what they think is the secret area and discover Borchert, apparently already entertaining someone.
jokes.punchline: The polite tea-party exchange in a secret underground bunker is played completely straight, the mundanity absurd against the dramatic intrusion.
jokes.explanation: The joke lives entirely in the contrast between the high-stakes drama (school board men breaking down a door) and the genteel tea exchange. It works as a tonal reset and character introduction for Borchert, though it's more of a 'the scene is funny' moment than a precisely crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so we're trapped in a 1970s time capsule. Let's stay calm and think this through logically.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What if we're here forever? What if this IS our life now?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: According to these newspapers, disco is the future of music and it's here to stay.

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: Agreed!

jokes.text: Nobody's been in here since the '70s. / How do you know? / The debate team topic is: 'Who's hotter, Elliott Gould or Donald Sutherland?' / Donald Sutherland. / Donald Sutherland.
jokes.setup: The group discovers the lost section of Greendale and speculates about how long it's been abandoned.
jokes.punchline: The 'proof' of its 1970s vintage is a chalkboard debate topic — and two characters immediately and independently answer 'Donald Sutherland' as if it's current and relevant.
jokes.explanation: Two-stage joke: the debate topic itself is a funny period artifact, but the real joke is that two separate characters instantly answer it without hesitation (and agree), implying they've both thought about this. The structure is excellent — setup delivers the period detail, the double 'Donald Sutherland' is the unexpected button. Good laugh construction.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, it's dangerous down there?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Of course it's dangerous. It's a sex dungeon.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's what they all say. Look, the key to survival is accepting that everything down there wants to hurt you, and just rolling with it. That's life, Britta.

jokes.text: If it's like a regular dungeon, it's only as dangerous as whoever invited you.
jokes.setup: Someone says the place is 'scary.' Shirley responds reassuringly.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's comfort is predicated on knowing what 'regular dungeons' are like — the calm expertise about dungeon etiquette from the prim, church-going Southern woman is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Community character subversion: Shirley's seemingly innocent response reveals unexpected familiarity with S&M dungeon culture. The joke works because it's delivered as genuine reassurance, not as a wink. The character integration is high — this would be less funny from anyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: If we encounter killer robots, how will we identify them?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: They'll be trying to kill us.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But how will we know they're robots?

jokes.text: Abed, if there's killer robots down here, you'll tell them we're on your side.
jokes.setup: The group cautiously explores the mysterious underground section. Jeff addresses Abed.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's request is based on the assumption that (a) killer robots might exist, and (b) Abed would have diplomatic relations with them — which Jeff treats as a reasonable working assumption.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's pragmatic acknowledgment of Abed's robot-whispering potential is a nice character moment — it also reveals that Jeff, for all his cynicism, has normalized Abed's unusual worldview enough to plan around it. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I don't know anything about the 70s. I was born in the 80s.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, I can help. The 70s were all about disco and bell bottoms.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Right, so we're looking for some groovy cat in some far out threads who's really getting down with his bad self?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: ...That's not how anyone talked.

jokes.text: Won't know them from ordinary robots until they kill us.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Abed to tell any killer robots they're on his side.
jokes.punchline: Abed's perfectly reasonable, matter-of-fact response: killer robots are indistinguishable from regular ones until the killing starts — so the plan has a fatal flaw.
jokes.explanation: Abed at his best: responding to an absurd premise with complete sincerity and an even MORE troubling logical point. The structure is a perfect deflation — Jeff's plan was comfort-seeking, Abed points out the fundamental flaw with zero affect. 'Until they kill us' as a matter-of-fact endpoint is the right dark note. High character integration because this response captures everything about how Abed processes information.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: My light is better, so I should lead.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous. My light is perfectly fine.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, it's not. Mine is objectively superior.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're an expert on lighting? That's so typical of you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: At least I'm not always wrong about everything.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what? You're being a total jerk right now.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, you're being stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm stupid? Says the guy who thinks his stupid light makes him a leader!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's not stupid, and you're the stupid one for not seeing it!

jokes.text: Split up. Leave no '70s reference unturned. This decade's out of my wheelhouse. Pet Rock, leave no Pet Rock unturned.
jokes.setup: The group needs to search the 1970s-era section. Abed directs the search.
jokes.punchline: Abed starts with 'leave no '70s reference unturned' — a clever meta idiom — then immediately reveals a gap in his encyclopedic knowledge: 'this decade's out of my wheelhouse,' and then tries to recover with 'Pet Rock' as his only 70s touchstone.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Abed — the bottomless pop-culture encyclopedia — has a decade he's unfamiliar with is a funny crack in his armor. The recovery attempt ('Pet Rock') with the modified idiom is a good button. Strong character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why are you crying?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: These beanbag chairs... they're from my childhood.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh man, you need better lumbar support? I know a guy.

jokes.text: Let me lead. My light's better. / You're that insecure that your light has to be better?
jokes.setup: The group descends into a dark area. Hickey insists on leading because his light is better.
jokes.punchline: Jeff weaponizes pop-psychology against a purely practical statement, turning a flashlight preference into a masculinity/insecurity issue.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's reflexive psychologizing of mundane situations is a reliable character beat. The joke is in the absurd leap from 'better flashlight' to 'masculinity complex.' Functional, character-specific, nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm worried we're falling apart. We won't even be a group anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're not falling apart. We're a TV show that's losing viewers. It happens. We'll get cancelled, go to streaming, or get rebooted with a different actor playing me.

jokes.text: It's just spider webs and beanbag chairs. / Don't cry. The importance of lumbar support hadn't—
jokes.setup: Someone reports that a room contains only spider webs and beanbag chairs. Shirley seems emotional.
jokes.punchline: Shirley appears to be crying about the beanbag chairs — and the response is to comfort her about the inadequacy of lumbar support in the 1970s, treating this as the obvious cause of tears.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist non-sequitur that works as a beat more than a crafted joke. The interruption of Shirley clarifying it's not about beanbag chairs suggests the writers are setting up something bigger. Mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jeff and Britta's Mediocre Adventure.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No wait - Jeff and Britta: A Study in Disappointment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: How about... Two Attractive People Make Questionable Decisions?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or we could go with Jeff and Britta's Ongoing Argument About Whether They're a Couple.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My personal favorite: Will They? Won't They? Does Anyone Care?

jokes.text: In Jeff and Britta's case, something that'd last six episodes, have bickering, starring them and an equally WASP-y couple, with a title like 'Better With My Worse Half' or 'Tying the Not.' 'Knot' is spelled without a K. Or #CouplePeopleProblems.
jokes.setup: Abed theorizes about why Jeff and Britta announced their engagement — he thinks they're 'spinning off into something safer.'
jokes.punchline: Abed predicts the exact title, format, and hashtag of a generic network sitcom that Jeff and Britta would star in — 'Tying the Not' (then self-correcting the pun), and '#CouplePeopleProblems' as a fake hashtag.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes: Abed is predicting the death of Community by imagining the safer, blander show that would replace it. 'Tying the Not' with the corrected spelling is excellent — the pun only half-works as written (intentionally), and the self-correction makes it funnier. '#CouplePeopleProblems' as a hashtag-era sitcom title is a perfect lampoon. This is Community at its most self-aware and anxious about its own survival. The craft is high because it works as genuine TV satire AND as character voice. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, it's 'Community.' The period is silent.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: #Community

jokes.text: Every episode, you decide who has— / Stop developing.
jokes.setup: Abed is pitch-developing the fake Jeff/Britta sitcom in real time, describing episode formats.
jokes.punchline: Annie cuts him off with 'Stop developing' — treating Abed's compulsive TV development as a recognized condition that needs to be addressed.
jokes.explanation: 'Stop developing' as a two-word command is excellent economy. It's funny because it treats Abed's TV-brain compulsion as a bad habit like biting nails. Good button on the previous joke.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We've been going in circles. Paintball episodes, blanket forts, saving the school from administrative incompetence. But here's the thing about shows like ours—they don't really end. They just go into syndication in your heart.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The network wants closure. The fans want more seasons. And I'm just here, aware that I'm in a sitcom, aware that I'm aware that I'm in a sitcom, which is itself a tired trope at this point.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So here's what happens: We say goodbye. You stop watching. And then in six months, you'll rewatch the pilot, remember why you loved this show, and we'll all pretend this ending never happened. That's not cynicism—that's just how television works.

jokes.text: I have a girlfriend. / What? / You were about to start a kiss lean. / I was not.
jokes.setup: Abed has just delivered a moving speech to Annie about their show not being over. A tender moment builds between them.
jokes.punchline: Before Annie can respond, Abed preemptively announces 'I have a girlfriend' — accurately reading a romantic lean that Annie flatly denies.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed: he can read a 'kiss lean' forming in real time and name it clinically before it happens. The comedic timing depends on this being a genuine emotional beat that Abed deflates with perfect precision. 'Fine. Let's find treasure.' as the capper is a great return to narrative. The character integration is excellent — this is Abed being socially aware in the most socially awkward possible way.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know what you're thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You do?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're wondering if this is the moment where we finally get together. Where the will-they-won't-they ends and we become a couple.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I... wasn't thinking that.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. Because it's not. I'm going to stop you before you start, because I've seen enough TV to know how this ends, and spoiler alert: it doesn't end well for us.

jokes.text: These basketball cards with white people on them.
jokes.setup: The group reports what 'treasures' they've found in the 1970s section.
jokes.punchline: Among the found objects are basketball cards featuring white players — the racial composition of the 1970s NBA presented as a quaint historical artifact.
jokes.explanation: A quick observational joke about the demographic history of professional basketball. Light and breezy, works as part of the '70s time-capsule montage. Nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so we found a bottle cap, three pennies, and a sock.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I found a coupon for yogurt that expired in 2003.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: There's a half-eaten sandwich in here. I don't know how old it is.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I found a photo of someone else's family vacation. Definitely not ours.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This instruction manual is for a VCR. Who even has those anymore?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I found a glass eye. Just... a glass eye. No explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: There's a restraining order with my name on it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Is that... is that a live possum?

jokes.text: Try every button. Just try every single button ever.
jokes.setup: The group proposes the jukebox might be the secret door key. Jeff has just said 'it's okay if we fail.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate complete reversal — going from resigned acceptance to frantically trying everything — undercuts his cool-guy pose perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-betrayal is the joke — he can't maintain his resigned-adult pose when adventure is possible. The phrasing 'every single button ever' is a good escalation. Decent character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Track 127? That's the one that makes the jukebox skip ahead seventeen tracks because of a electromagnetic pulse it creates in the mechanism.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not how jukeboxes work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You're right, I was thinking of track 128.

jokes.text: Are you all right? / No! I was dying!
jokes.setup: Duncan is apparently struggling with something (the aftereffects of his electrocution).
jokes.punchline: The check-in 'are you all right?' gets the maximally dramatic response — 'No! I was dying!' — delivered with full British indignation.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Duncan's electrocution that keeps the running gag alive. The joke is in the past tense ('I WAS dying') — not a present crisis but a grievance. Functional, not exceptional.

jokes.text: Try track 127. / Right. Because 127 in binary code would be a palindrome. / Because the song title is 'Open the Door' by the Secret Doors.
jokes.setup: The group needs to open a secret door via jukebox. Borchert suggests track 127.
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately constructs a hyper-specific binary palindrome justification — but Borchert corrects him: the reason is simply that the song is called 'Open the Door' by the Secret Doors.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best pure structural joke. Setup: track 127. Abed's mind immediately leaps to an elaborate binary-palindrome justification. Punchline: the actual reason is literal and completely obvious — a song called 'Open the Door.' It's a double deflation: (1) Abed's pattern-seeking intelligence is subverted, and (2) Borchert's eccentric genius turns out to be just very literal. It also characterizes both men perfectly. The binary palindrome detail is specific enough to seem real (127 in binary IS 1111111, which IS a palindrome), making Abed's reasoning plausible and the joke smarter. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So, uh, there's been some changes since the '70s. Michael Jackson turned white, O.J. Simpson killed his wife, and Woody Allen married his adopted daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But hey, at least we still have Woody Allen movies to look forward to... oh wait, no we don't.

jokes.text: Try track 127. / Right. Because 127 in binary code would be a palindrome. / Because the song title is 'Open the Door' by the Secret Doors.
jokes.setup: The group is trying to figure out which jukebox track opens the secret door
jokes.punchline: Abed provides two completely different types of reasoning for the same number — one is false (127 in binary is not a palindrome, it's 1111111) and delivered with confidence, one is literalist (the song is literally called 'Open the Door'). The group accepts both.
jokes.explanation: Two-tier joke: Abed provides pseudo-intellectual coding logic (which is actually wrong, a potential meta-joke about Abed's confidence exceeding accuracy), and then the actual reason is sublimely literal — the song is called 'Open the Door.' The layering rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I don't know what's happening to me. I can't control it.

jokes.text: ♪ OPEN THE DOOR / WE GOT TO OPEN THE DOOR / AND THE DOOR IS OPENING / YOU'RE PLAYING THE SONG THAT OPENS THE DOOR / WE RECORDED THIS SONG FOR WHEN YOU OPEN THE DOOR / SPECIALLY TIMED TO THE DURATION OF THE OPENING PROCESS ♪
jokes.setup: Track 127 is played. It opens the secret door.
jokes.punchline: The song is a purely functional, self-narrating piece of music that describes its own purpose in real time — 'specially timed to the duration of the opening process.'
jokes.explanation: The song payoff is excellent: it escalates from a simple title-matching gag to a song that is entirely self-aware of its own function. 'We recorded this song for when you open the door / Specially timed to the duration of the opening process' is a beautiful absurdist joke — a song that acknowledges its own existence as a prop. The commitment to the bit (it has actual lyrics, it's timed to the door) elevates it. This is the kind of joke Community does uniquely well.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: I lose track of how big I'm getting.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce Hawthorne
dialogue.line: We're keeping very close track.

jokes.text: Okay, I'm gonna peel off some Band-Aids here. Dennis Hopper is dead. TV shows give no time for theme songs anymore. And Woody Allen did the voice of a cartoon ant.
jokes.setup: The group has found Borchert alive in his bunker after 50 years. Jeff prepares to deliver news about the outside world.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's selection of the three most important facts to update Borchert with: Dennis Hopper's death, the decline of TV theme songs, and Woody Allen voicing Antz — presented in that order of significance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and highly quotable. The humor has three layers: (1) of all the things that happened in 50 years, these are Jeff's chosen highlights; (2) the escalating weirdness — death, TV production changes, and then Antz as the capstone; (3) each item is oddly specific and evocative. The Woody Allen/Antz choice is the perfect anti-climax that somehow loops back to being profound. This is very Jeff — culturally curated, slightly defensive, oddly sincere. The structure (escalating importance with a strange third act) is perfect. Near-landmark joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, what was that game called again?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hawkthorne.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Never mind, I'm out.

jokes.text: Jeff! / Sorry, I lose track of how big I'm getting.
jokes.setup: Jeff apparently makes a dramatic physical gesture or expands his chest/posture while delivering news to Borchert, and someone has to call him out.
jokes.punchline: 'I lose track of how big I'm getting' — Jeff's narcissistic relationship with his own body presented as an unintentional side effect.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's vanity about his body is a running character trait, and 'I lose track of how big I'm getting' as an inadvertent reveal of obsessive mirror-checking is sharp. The delivery of this as a sincere explanation rather than a brag makes it funnier — he's not proud, he's just reporting a known problem. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Who's a smart boy? You're a smart boy! Yes you are!

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: Stop it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Does someone need a nappy change? Is it nap time?

jokes.text: I don't. (re: losing track of how big Jeff is getting)
jokes.setup: Jeff says he loses track of how big he's getting.
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat 'I don't' — an inadvertent admission that she tracks Jeff's physical development — is delivered straight.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum joke. Annie's 'I don't' accidentally reveals that she is very aware of Jeff's body — which plays into their long-running will-they-won't-they dynamic. The economy is perfect: she doesn't elaborate, she doesn't walk it back. It just sits there. The rewatch bonus is real because it hits differently knowing Annie's feelings about Jeff throughout the series. This is a 'best joke of the episode' contender because of its extraordinary economy and the layers it contains.

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: They went to execute the plan.

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: We're meeting at that Thai place on 5th Street. You know, the one with the red awning? They have an excellent pad thai, but more importantly, their spring rolls come with three different dipping sauces, and one of them is a mystery sauce that I'm 73% confident is just mayo mixed with sriracha.

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: Troy's gonna create a diversion by pretending to be a health inspector. Abed will film it for his documentary about pretending to be things. Pierce will say something racist by accident. Shirley will get angry. Jeff will try to fix it with his face. And Annie will somehow end up with a clipboard.

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: It's foolproof. We'll all meet back at that Thai place by 7, split an order of the crab rangoon—which, again, inexplicably delicious—and nobody will ever know we were here.

jokes.text: You guys are the worst, with your stupid paintballs and your freeze tags. / Hot Lava. / That was Hot Lava? Dumb.
jokes.setup: The school board men confront the group and list the absurd things they've done to the school.
jokes.punchline: The school board calls out 'Hot Lava' (a beloved fan-favorite Community episode concept) as 'dumb' — essentially letting the antagonists voice what some critics thought of the show's high-concept episodes.
jokes.explanation: Community has the courage to put 'that was dumb' in the mouth of characters about its own beloved high-concept episodes. The beat where someone says 'Hot Lava' and Carl responds 'That was Hot Lava? Dumb' is a self-deprecating meta-move. Reward for long-time viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have stolen your brain! I have stolen your brain!

jokes.text: You're special, Richie. Your mind is special. You know it works differently from other kids' minds. / Richie's a freak, Richie's a freak.
jokes.setup: Borchert has apparently used his feelings-computer to read Richie's mind and is now exploiting a childhood trauma to manipulate him.
jokes.punchline: Borchert leads Richie through what appears to be a repressed memory — 'You're special' followed by the childhood taunt — sending Richie into a vulnerable emotional state Borchert then exploits.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy: Borchert weaponizing childhood trauma for tactical advantage is funny precisely because it's played as a cool skill rather than an ethical concern. The juxtaposition of the gentle 'your mind is special' with the childlike taunting voice is effective cringe-comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: So how are you going to find all this equipment? It's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'll find it. I always do.

jokes.text: They climbed out to the roof, hopped on a hang glider and flew it across town to that Greek restaurant. Papa Cristo's?
jokes.setup: Borchert has just read Richie's mind. Carl asks if he knows where the group went.
jokes.punchline: Borchert confidently reads a completely fabricated memory — the group apparently escaped via hang glider to a named Greek restaurant — with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Papa Cristo's' as the hang glider destination is what makes this joke great — Borchert invents a hyper-specific false memory, complete with a real-sounding restaurant name. The confidence of delivery is key. This is classic absurdist comedy: the more specific and wrong the detail, the funnier it is.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Even down here, completely isolated underground, we couldn't escape the 1980s.

jokes.text: I robbed your brain. I robbed it.
jokes.setup: Borchert has successfully manipulated Richie using the feelings-computer. He explains what just happened.
jokes.punchline: 'I robbed your brain. I robbed it.' — the casual, slightly gleeful admission that he just committed cognitive theft, repeated for emphasis.
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'I robbed it' — using petty-theft language for cognitive manipulation — is perfectly eccentric Borchert. The repetition ('I robbed it') adds an oddly childlike satisfaction that makes the character funnier. Very quotable because it's a novel phrase for a novel concept.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: I've got some leftover money I can contribute to help save Greendale.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: But I should warn you - this is from 2003, so it's only worth about 60% of face value now.

jokes.text: Was there a hang glider? / You're gonna find a hang glider down there. That much I know.
jokes.setup: Carl hears that the group went through a hatch. He asks Borchert — who just made up the hang glider story — if the hang glider is relevant.
jokes.punchline: Borchert, without missing a beat, commits to the hang glider detail — 'That much I know' — as if it's genuinely reliable information from his brain-robbery.
jokes.explanation: The callback elevates the original joke. Borchert doubling down on a clearly invented detail — with added authority ('That much I know') — is structurally excellent. The confidence of the wrong commitment is funnier than the original fabrication. Good escalation of the absurdist thread.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Well, money is worth what money is worth.

jokes.text: So anyway, I sealed myself up down here with 50 years of food, 50 years of toilet paper, and 50 years of cocaine — which I somehow ran out of after about 10 years.
jokes.setup: Borchert explains how he survived underground for 50 years.
jokes.punchline: The list of provisions escalates to 'cocaine,' and then Borchert reveals he burned through 50 years' worth in 10 — the understatement 'somehow ran out of' doing all the work.
jokes.explanation: Classic Community escalation joke. The structure is perfect: food, toilet paper (practical), cocaine (the reveal), and then 'which I somehow ran out of after about 10 years.' The word 'somehow' is doing incredible work — it's false bewilderment about an obvious outcome. The structure follows the rule of three and then subverts it with a fourth beat (the usage note). Very high quotability. One of the episode's top-tier jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You hear that, computer? I've got a pickle, and I'm not afraid to use it!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That's right. A pickle. The computer's natural enemy.

jokes.text: The '80s happened down here too.
jokes.setup: Borchert has just said he ran out of 50 years of cocaine in 10 years.
jokes.punchline: 'The '80s happened down here too' — an entire decade of excess summarized as a simple, matter-of-fact statement.
jokes.explanation: Six words, maximum impact. This is a masterclass in comedic economy — the entire '80s drug culture is summarized with no editorializing. The deadpan delivery of 'The '80s happened down here too' as an explanation/excuse is perfect. It works as a standalone line AND as a perfect button to the previous cocaine joke. One of the best-constructed brief jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, where's my mask?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm not crazy. I'm just a little mentally ill.

jokes.text: Sir, Raquel has taken the best years of your life and a dozen of your not-so-good. If she hasn't given anything back, it might be time to move on.
jokes.setup: Borchert is emotionally attached to Raquel (his computer). Jeff tries to convince him to let the group use/cannibalize her.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a sincere-sounding relationship speech about 'moving on' from a one-sided partnership — but he's talking about a computer. The relationship-counseling register applied to human-machine codependency is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's ability to give earnest speech-therapy advice to a man about his computer is both funny and very Jeff — he's always delivering big speeches. The 'dozen of your not-so-good' is a nicely specific dig that elevates it above a generic breakup speech.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Look! Look at that! Did you see that? It responded to my emotional output! The screen flickered just slightly. See? See how the pixels shifted infinitesimally? That's acknowledgment. That's connection.

jokes.text: I don't think it's worth much. Those are Gerald Ford dollars. / How many? / Couple of million. / Back in the '70s, that was worth millions.
jokes.setup: Borchert reveals he has leftover cash under his desk. He dismisses its value.
jokes.punchline: He specifies 'Gerald Ford dollars' (implying currency somehow tied to a specific president), and then when asked how much, says 'couple of million' — immediately followed by clarifying 'back in the '70s, that was worth millions.' (Which is obvious — a couple of million IS worth millions.)
jokes.explanation: The 'Gerald Ford dollars' is a funny invented currency detail — the kind of Borchert-specific eccentricity that builds character. The clarification 'back in the '70s, that was worth millions' is a beautiful tautology — he's restating the obvious as if it's a caveat, suggesting he's slightly confused about how inflation works (or doesn't) in his bunker-time.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: What are these little faces people keep using?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Those are emoticons. They help convey tone in text.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Ah, I see. So a colon and parenthesis makes a smile. How perfectly accurate but utterly pointless.

jokes.text: Get back. This pickle's a magnet. / I'll wipe her out, man. / Don't you dare use that on her!
jokes.setup: Chang reveals himself as a villain and threatens Raquel the computer with a pickle.
jokes.punchline: Chang's villain weapon is a magnet disguised as a pickle. Borchert's horror at the threat is completely sincere.
jokes.explanation: A pickle that's a magnet is a great absurdist villain-weapon choice — specific, low-tech, and ridiculous. Borchert's protective rage over his computer makes it funnier. Chang threatening someone with a pickle while delivering a line like 'I'll wipe her out, man' is peak Chang chaos energy.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no. No, no, no, no, no. It's true. It's all true. The idiots... they've won. They've actually won.

jokes.text: Chang, you've become a bad guy again? / There's a lot more to it than that, Britta.
jokes.setup: Chang reveals he's working with the school board against the group. Britta calls him out.
jokes.punchline: Chang suggests his villainy has depth and nuance — but then immediately contradicts himself.
jokes.explanation: Chang's claim of complexity is set up for immediate deflation. Gets a solid laugh from anyone who's followed Chang's chaotic alignment throughout the series.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: You need to restart the computer with human emotion. I use nipple stimulation as my emotional baseline.

jokes.text: Wait, I'm not wearing a mask? / There's no more to it. I think I'm just mentally ill.
jokes.setup: Chang claimed there's 'a lot more to it' — implying his villainy has depth.
jokes.punchline: Chang checks if he's wearing a mask (suggesting he might be a different character), then gives up and admits: 'I think I'm just mentally ill.' — a sincere, self-aware diagnosis that retroactively explains everything.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's finest jokes. 'Wait, I'm not wearing a mask?' is a perfect absurdist beat — Chang checking for a mask implies that in his world, villain reveals often come with masks, and his genuine uncertainty about his own face is deeply funny. 'I think I'm just mentally ill' as the resolution is brilliant: it's simultaneously self-aware commentary on how the writers have treated Chang's character arc AND a sincere attempt at explanation. The 'I think' qualifier is the key — he's not certain even about this. Near-landmark character moment for a secondary character.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Everyone, meet our new Vice Dean, Russell Borchert.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Thank you, Dean. I'm excited to embrace this institution's digital future. I've been reading about this 'Facebook' thing. Remarkable innovation.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Facebook's been around for like fifteen years.

dialogue.speaker: Russell Borchert
dialogue.line: Precisely. Revolutionary.

jokes.text: So we're trapped in here forever. / Or just until we run out of food and water. / At least we'll have each other. / Till death do us part.
jokes.setup: Raquel is destroyed and the door is stuck. The group processes that they're trapped.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'trapped forever' to the specific doom condition (food/water), the false comfort ('at least we'll have each other'), and then Jeff/Britta's callback to their marriage announcement with 'till death do us part' — played as a grim punchline.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed dark-comedy beat with a callback. The 'till death do us part' lands as the best button to their engagement storyline because it's the first wedding vow that suddenly has very literal application. Good structure and callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Subway Rep
dialogue.line: We've made the difficult decision to realign our institutional partnerships with a focus on core market optimization and stakeholder value proposition.

dialogue.speaker: All Subway Reps
dialogue.line: Eat fresh!

jokes.text: You know what? You guys can have my food and water.
jokes.setup: The group notes they'll be trapped until food and water run out. This is a crisis.
jokes.punchline: Borchert immediately offers his supplies — but delivered as such a casual, resigned non-offer that it implies: (a) he was planning to die anyway, or (b) he's just a very weird person.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that characterizes Borchert's detachment from normal survival instincts. Light laugh, functional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, Greendale's been on the chopping block since I got here. It's like our default state. We could probably get a bulk discount on the guillotine at this point.

jokes.text: You know what? You guys can have my food and water.
jokes.setup: The group has just realized they're trapped and will die of thirst/hunger; there's a beat of despair
jokes.punchline: Borchert's response to the group's existential panic is a casual offer to give them his supplies — suggesting he either has no survival instinct or doesn't value his own continued existence, delivered with complete nonchalance
jokes.explanation: Borchert treating his own survival supplies as an inconsequential offering is consistent with his character — a man who has been alone for 50 years and seems comfortable with almost any outcome. The deadpan delivery of a genuinely magnanimous but alarming offer is good Borchert characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I wasn't electrocuted, I was shocked. Electrocution is when you're killed by electricity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, but you're kind of proving my point about why nobody likes you.

jokes.text: Oh, thank God. Her emotional components are still online. / Emotional components?
jokes.setup: The group is despairing; Borchert checks on Raquel
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the computer has emotional components (as opposed to logical ones) — and that the emotional components survived while logical ones presumably didn't — is both a plot point and a commentary on Borchert's priorities and design philosophy
jokes.explanation: Jeff's bewildered 'Emotional components?' is a good reaction beat. The setup-reaction structure works because it's both plot-relevant and reveals the absurdity of Borchert's computer design philosophy (feelings first, logic optional).

dialogue.speaker: Richie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was just thinking about hang gliders the whole time.

jokes.text: It's a video of a kitten. / And why are those people arguing about it? / And what's that? / An emoticon. That person wants to indicate happiness but can't convey it with language, so they misuse punctuation to form a smile. / That is so— / Stupid. / Only an idiot would think of this. / Idiots won!
jokes.setup: Borchert is shown modern internet for the first time. He sees a kitten video and comment section arguments, then emoticons.
jokes.punchline: Borchert, who built a computer to process human emotion, discovers the internet — and concludes 'Idiots won!' as his assessment of the digital age, following from his realization that his mission ('idiots with feelings' won over 'emotionless eggheads') has succeeded.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's thematic centerpieces and a great joke: Borchert's decades-long mission was to prevent emotionless logic from dominating over human feeling. He concludes from kitten videos and emoticons that 'idiots won' — which is both depressing AND exactly what he wanted. 'Idiots won!' as a triumphant declaration is very quotable and captures something true about internet culture with one phrase. The comedic arc from his serious technological philosophy to 'idiots won' is well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is, technically, none of us have a legitimate claim to Greendale because it was built on Native American land?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but let's not get into that rabbit hole.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm serious. If we're going to argue over who owns this place, shouldn't we at least acknowledge that the real owners were here first?

jokes.text: It's a video of a kitten. / And why are those people arguing about it? / And what's that? / An emoticon. That person wants to indicate happiness but can't convey it with language, so they misuse punctuation to form a smile.
jokes.setup: Borchert is shown the modern internet for the first time; he sees a cat video and a comment section argument.
jokes.punchline: Borchert's clinical description of an emoticon — 'that person wants to indicate happiness but can't convey it with language, so they misuse punctuation to form a smile' — is funnier than any mockery because it's completely accurate and devastating.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Borchert's detached, analytical description of internet culture as if observing a strange animal. The emoticon definition ('misuse punctuation to form a smile') is an incredibly precise, slightly contemptuous framing that makes the act of using emoticons sound pathetic and desperate. Borchert as internet anthropologist is a great comedic perspective.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: As a member of the school board, I'm going to use my newfound authority to demand that the cafeteria serve only foods shaped like my face.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Chang, you've been on the board for twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And? The people have spoken. Well, I have spoken. I am the people now.

jokes.text: That is so... / Stupid. / Only an idiot would think of this. / Idiots won! / Which means my work down here is done.
jokes.setup: Borchert is reacting to seeing internet culture — the audience and Jeff expect him to be horrified or delighted
jokes.punchline: Borchert calls the internet stupid, calls its creators idiots — but then declares 'idiots won' as a triumph, because his life's work was proving that idiots (people driven by feelings rather than logic) would dominate technology. His work is done.
jokes.explanation: One of the best thematic jokes in the episode. The misdirection is perfect: we expect wonder or horror at the internet, but instead get a vindication of Borchert's thesis — his prediction that emotionally-driven idiots would dominate technology has been confirmed by cat videos and emoticons. 'Idiots won!' is a triumphant declaration that also functions as a devastating critique of internet culture. The payoff of his entire life's work being confirmed by a kitten video is exceptional comedy writing with genuine thematic resonance.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We'll be back next year.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Unless the show gets cancelled.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or unless NBC decides to move us to a different time slot, which would destroy our ratings.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or unless our lead actor gets a movie deal and decides to leave mid-season.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or unless the writers' room burns down in a freak accident involving a malfunctioning coffee maker and a stack of scripts.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Or unless the entire cast is abducted by aliens who mistake us for the Real Housewives cast.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But canon-wise, we're definitely coming back.

jokes.text: ...but that's only if somebody in this room has feelings stronger than I get when I rub my nipples — so good luck with that, folks.
jokes.setup: Borchert explains that to restart Raquel, they need a blast of human passion. He sets the bar for what 'strong enough emotion' means.
jokes.punchline: He calibrates the emotional threshold as 'stronger than I get when I rub my nipples' — a very specific, personal, and deeply weird benchmark.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most memorable jokes. The specificity of 'rub my nipples' as a calibration point for emotional intensity is exactly the right level of weird for Borchert — it's intimate, eccentric, and weirdly sincere. The 'so good luck with that, folks' as a dismissive sign-off suggests he doesn't believe any of them can clear the bar, which makes the eventual resolution funnier. High originality because nobody has set a 'nipple rubbing' emotional threshold before on network television. Earns its near-top score.

jokes.text: Give me that. Everybody over there. Turn around. Turn around now.
jokes.setup: Borchert has just said they need someone with extremely strong feelings to restart the computer. Jeff grabs something and orders everyone to turn around.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate decisive action — grabbing something and commanding privacy — implies he knows exactly what he's going to do (a moment of extreme emotional vulnerability) and refuses to have an audience. The joke is what's NOT shown.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap: Jeff's pride is so enormous that he would rather die trapped underground than display vulnerability in front of his friends. His commandeering of the moment and demand for privacy tells us everything — and the audience immediately understands what he's about to do (think about Annie, presumably). The character integration is near-perfect because only Jeff would handle emotional vulnerability as a tactical military operation.

jokes.text: You're here to save me, aren't you? / Let's get out of here and never look back.
jokes.setup: Jeff has turned to Annie in his moment of emotional need. Annie asks if he's here to save her.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response — 'Let's get out of here and never look back' — is the most emotionally constipated possible response to a romantic moment. He can generate feelings but can't name them.
jokes.explanation: The humor here is in Jeff's emotional evasiveness dressed up as action-movie dialogue. 'Never look back' is cinematic bluster that also literally means 'let's not examine this emotionally.' Good character moment, secondary laugh.

jokes.text: In case you have to remember me, can I give you quotes? / Shut up, Abed. / Milady. / Milord.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Annie are having a moment. Abed, still present, asks if he can deliver quotes for them to remember him by — in case this is the end.
jokes.punchline: Shut up, Abed. Then: Milady/Milord — Jeff and Annie exchange an absurdly formal archaic farewell that is both tender and ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke with two different punchlines. First, Abed's bid to deliver memorable last words is immediately shut down — the meta-awareness of his own quotability is funny and sad. Then 'Milady/Milord' between Jeff and Annie is the perfect tonal button: it's their romantic shorthand rendered in the most grandiose possible form. The archaic formality as expression of genuine feeling is both absurd and touching — peak Community tone. High quotability, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: What did you do? / Don't worry about it. Let's go.
jokes.setup: The door opens. The group emerges. Someone asks Jeff what he did to restart the computer.
jokes.punchline: Jeff refuses to explain — 'Don't worry about it' — the defensive deflection of a man who just had to show deep vulnerability and will never speak of it.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'turn around' joke is Jeff's total emotional shutdown post-vulnerability. 'Don't worry about it' is the right response from Jeff — it's simultaneously dismissive and revealing. Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: Objection. I teach law at Greendale, so believe me — I don't know much about law.
jokes.setup: Jeff interrupts the school sale ceremony with 'Objection.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own legal authority: 'I teach law at Greendale, so believe me — I don't know much about law.' The credential IS the disqualification.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The structure of 'I teach X at Greendale, so believe me, I don't know much about X' is a perfect double inversion: normally a credential builds credibility; here, the credential is at Greendale, which guarantees incompetence. The 'so believe me' as a trust-building pivot into a confession of ignorance is structurally brilliant. Only works fully with Jeff's character — a former lawyer who has never respected Greendale — but the construction is tight enough to be funny cold.

jokes.text: This is a legitimate transaction where a city is selling a school to a restaurant. It happens somewhere every day.
jokes.setup: Jeff objects to the sale. The city official defends the transaction.
jokes.punchline: 'It happens somewhere every day' — delivered as if city-to-restaurant school sales are a routine, unremarkable occurrence.
jokes.explanation: Deadpan defense of the indefensible: treating an absurd premise as mundane routine. 'It happens somewhere every day' is the right level of confident wrongness. Good economy.

jokes.text: So Subway Sandwich University — meet your new vice dean, Russell Borchert.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals Borchert's founder status and argues it blocks the sale.
jokes.punchline: He introduces Borchert to the assembled suits as 'your new vice dean' — the reveal that the eccentric bunker-hermit will now be in leadership of the renamed Subway university.
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands as a satisfying plot joke rather than a pure comedy moment — the humor is situational (Borchert, visually insane, is now their administrative partner). Functions well as a crowd-pleasing scene beat.

jokes.text: Hi. I guess we're gonna be partners. I understand there's some Internet where I can make my inner thoughts public.
jokes.setup: Borchert is introduced to the Subway executives as their new vice dean. He introduces himself.
jokes.punchline: Borchert's first priority upon entering the modern world is expressing himself on 'some Internet' — his description of social media as 'making inner thoughts public' is simultaneously accurate and deeply sad.
jokes.explanation: Borchert's characterization continues: his interest in 'some Internet' and his flat description of social media's purpose ('make inner thoughts public') is both funny and a sharp social observation. The vagueness of 'some Internet' is a good fish-out-of-water detail.

jokes.text: We do good food at good prices. We are but simple sandwich artists who want the world to eat fresh. / Eat fresh!
jokes.setup: The Subway executives back down from the conflict.
jokes.punchline: Their retreat is phrased entirely in Subway marketing slogans, culminating in the actual 'Eat Fresh!' tagline — the corporate voice as a character limitation.
jokes.explanation: Community has had a long meta-relationship with Subway (a character named 'Subway' appeared in earlier seasons), so using Subway's actual slogans as corporate-speak has earned context. The 'Eat fresh!' button is a satisfying payoff to the season-long Subway subplot. Gets a knowing laugh from longtime viewers.

jokes.text: No! No, you did not. You moved dirt around Greendale's grave. Your school is still bankrupt, it is still unmarketable, and it is still on the permanent chopping block of anyone who has any say in its future.
jokes.setup: The group asks 'Did we just save Greendale?' with triumphant music. Richie deflates the moment.
jokes.punchline: 'You moved dirt around Greendale's grave.' — the specific, literary brutality of this image delivered by the bureaucratic villain is unexpectedly poetic and devastating.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier lines in the episode's final act because it comes from Richie — a minor antagonist who is suddenly given a great line. 'Moved dirt around Greendale's grave' is a specifically vivid metaphor that's both mean and accurate, and it works as meta-commentary on the show's perpetual cliffhanger status. The humor is dark and self-aware.

jokes.text: Yeah? Well, around here, we call that Wednesday.
jokes.setup: Richie tells the group that nothing has really changed — Greendale is still doomed.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's comeback normalizes existential institutional crisis as a weekly occurrence — 'around here, we call that Wednesday.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines — high economy, great structure, and perfect character voice. 'Around here, we call that Wednesday' works on multiple levels: it's Jeff's cool-under-pressure persona, it's true about Greendale, and it's a quietly profound statement about the show's premise (a school perpetually on the verge of collapse, populated by people who keep showing up anyway). The 'around here' grounds it in community identity. Highly quotable and works as a thesis statement for the entire series. Near-benchmark joke.

jokes.text: Hey, after I was electrocuted, didn't you two say you were gonna get married? / Doesn't electrocuted technically mean killed? / You always have to correct people? / You always have to police correcting? / Marriage is off. / I think you mean the wedding is off. / Yeah!
jokes.setup: Post-rescue, Duncan reminds the group of the engagement announcement that happened during the chaos.
jokes.punchline: Three jokes in rapid sequence: Duncan's 'electrocuted technically means killed' pedantry; meta-commentary on correcting correctors; and the precision distinction between 'marriage' and 'wedding' being immediately embraced by the corrected party.
jokes.explanation: A dense multi-layer joke that callbacks to two earlier jokes simultaneously. Duncan the pedant correcting 'electrocuted' (following his earlier aluminium correction) is a perfect running gag payoff. The meta-correction spiral ('you always have to correct people' / 'you always have to police correcting') is well-constructed. And the Jeff/Britta engagement being dissolved through a semantic distinction ('the wedding is off' vs 'marriage is off') with someone cheering the correction is a brilliant comedic beat. This sequence rewards the whole episode's setup.

jokes.text: Hey, I gotta say, you held up well under that interrogation. / I'm gonna tell you something that I'd like to stay between us... I was thinking about a hang glider.
jokes.setup: Borchert compliments Richie on holding up under the brain-robbery. Richie confides something.
jokes.punchline: Richie admits he was actually thinking about a hang glider — confirming that Borchert's 'robbery' may have surfaced a genuine fantasy, not false information.
jokes.explanation: The hang glider callback pays off beautifully: Borchert's confident wrong information turns out to be right because it matched what Richie was actually thinking. This retroactively vindicates both Borchert's brain-robbery AND his doubling down. The 'I'd like to stay between us' makes Richie's admission feel like a genuine secret, adding a layer of absurd intimacy. Great callback structure.

jokes.text: None of this conflict truly matters. The only owners of this land are the Arapaho. Would it offend you if I asked you to train me in the use of certain powers?
jokes.setup: The dust has settled. Carl seems to be having a small revelation.
jokes.punchline: Carl's sudden acknowledgment of Native land rights pivots immediately to a request to be trained in Arapaho 'powers' — a concept he's just invented in his own head, treating the land rights acknowledgment as a networking opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Dark subversive comedy: Carl's awareness of colonial history immediately becomes colonialism again ('train me in certain powers'). The genuine remorse in the first sentence makes the second sentence funnier. The 'would it offend you' as false sensitivity before the offensive request is well-structured.

jokes.text: Sorry, Carl. You deserve better. Chang, you get it. How would you like a job on the school board? / Your first job is to deliver this to the City Bursar's Office.
jokes.setup: Richie fires Carl and immediately replaces him with Chang.
jokes.punchline: Chang is offered a job and immediately given an errand — the grand 'job offer' deflated to 'deliver this envelope.'
jokes.explanation: Light gag — Chang's new prestigious position immediately reduced to courier work. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Sorry, Carl. You deserve better. Chang, you get it. How would you like a job on the school board? / Your first job is to deliver this... to the City Bursar's Office. / On it.
jokes.setup: In the aftermath, Richie is reassigning positions; Carl has been let go
jokes.punchline: Chang is immediately hired onto the school board and given his first assignment — but it's just a delivery errand, suggesting 'school board member' is a low-stakes job, and Chang accepts it with complete enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Chang's immediate and unquestioning acceptance of a job that is literally just a delivery run reveals both the school board's low standards and Chang's pathetic eagerness for any institutional affiliation. Character-consistent but not exceptionally crafted.

jokes.text: Hi, yes, I'd like to replace all my teeth with diamonds.
jokes.setup: Chang has been given the envelope to deliver. He apparently makes a phone call instead.
jokes.punchline: Chang's first use of his new position/resources is calling to inquire about full diamond dental replacement.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chang absurdism: given any kind of power or resource, he immediately misappropriates it for a spectacularly weird personal goal. 'Replace all my teeth with diamonds' is a great specific absurd aspiration — not one tooth, ALL teeth — and the matter-of-fact phone inquiry delivery makes it funnier. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Hi, yes, I'd like to replace all my teeth with diamonds.
jokes.setup: Borchert has just received the Gerald Ford dollars windfall from his vault
jokes.punchline: His first planned expenditure is full dental diamond replacement — combining vanity, '70s excess, and the specific madness of a man who has been alone for 50 years deciding how to spend his money
jokes.explanation: Perfectly reveals Borchert's character priorities — a man obsessed with gold and emotion and isolation is now rich and his first instinct is total diamond dental replacement. It's specific, absurd, deeply in-character (gold is a conductor of emotion; diamonds are the next level), and very quotable.

jokes.text: We live to fight another day. / I never got a chance to wish you a happy birthday. Or Halloween or Christmas, or any specific calendar event.
jokes.setup: The group celebrates their temporary victory. Borchert offers a farewell.
jokes.punchline: Borchert's attempt at warm seasonal greetings covers every possible calendar event in lieu of knowing which applies — the maximally inclusive acknowledgment of time's passage.
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny: Borchert compensating for 50 years of missed social rituals by firing off all calendar events. 'Or any specific calendar event' as the catch-all is a good button. Character-specific but minor.

jokes.text: Well, maybe next year. / Definitely. We'll definitely be back next year. If not, it'll be because an asteroid has destroyed all human civilisation — and that's canon.
jokes.setup: The group talks about next year. Abed confirms they'll be back.
jokes.punchline: Abed's guarantee of returning is qualified with 'unless an asteroid destroys civilization — and that's canon' — a show-bible declaration that this is the ONLY acceptable reason for cancellation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest meta jokes and among the best of Community's self-referential moments. 'That's canon' is the key: Abed is designating narrative fact within the show's universe — the only way this show ends is if the entire world ends. This is simultaneously Community's defiance of cancellation anxiety AND Abed's most revealing character moment (he controls the narrative by declaring facts 'canon'). The 'What? Nothing.' deflection when others notice he said something odd is perfect. This is what Community does that no other show does: meta-commentary that is ALSO deep character comedy. Comparable in quality to the best examples in the taxonomy.

jokes.text: Penny for your thoughts.
jokes.setup: Post-credits or end scene. Someone asks Jeff what he's thinking.
jokes.punchline: The question itself — 'penny for your thoughts' — hangs in the air as the camera presumably catches Jeff in a rare moment of sincere reflection, the cliché phrase rendered oddly moving.
jokes.explanation: Ambiguous beat — this reads as a sweet coda rather than a punch-out joke. Minimal craft but serves the ending well. Rewatch bonus for seeing what Jeff is presumably thinking about (Annie, the future).

jokes.text: Intensive Karen. / Mr. Egypt. / Celebrity Beat-Off. / Captain Cook. / Depends on what fails.
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag: the group appears to be pitching fake TV show titles or game names to each other.
jokes.punchline: A rapid list of absurdist non-sequitur names ('Intensive Karen,' 'Celebrity Beat-Off,' 'Captain Cook') culminating in 'Depends on what fails' — which is either a title or a genuine production note, indistinguishable from the others.
jokes.explanation: Classic Community tag: a list of absurd invented titles with zero context. 'Celebrity Beat-Off' is the standout (deliberately ambiguous title) and 'Depends on what fails' is the perfect button — it sounds both like a title AND like a genuine answer to 'what should we do next.' Light but charming.

tmdb_overview: To save Greendale from being sold, the gang searches for an eccentric computer science professor's legendary treasure hidden beneath the school.
insight: Lean episode coasts on character chemistry—74 score from personality dynamics, not structural comedy.
